description: Use when ARC grids show colored diagonal stripes; infer a repeating diagonal color cycle and fill the grid.

# ARC diagonal-periodic fill

Use when the input contains sparse colored cells arranged along diagonals running down-right (constant `column - row`) and the target likely expands the pattern.

## Method
1. Record each colored clue as diagonal index `d = (column - row) mod n`, where `n` is the candidate cycle length.
2. Infer the smallest consistent period from repeated/parallel stripe clues. Map each residue to its color; clue cells should agree whenever their diagonal indices are congruent modulo the period.
3. Check the candidate against every clue, including diagonals that wrap across the grid modulo the period. Sparse clue regions may supply different parts of the cycle.
4. Fill every output cell `(r,c)` with the color assigned to `(c-r) mod n`. Keep the original grid dimensions.
5. Before submitting, verify all original nonzero clue cells are preserved and that each diagonal of a given residue has the same color.

## Pitfalls
- Use down-right diagonals, not rows/columns or anti-diagonals: these are constant `c-r`.
- The color cycle may be shorter than the grid width; do not assume each visible stripe corresponds to a unique infinite diagonal.
- Establish cycle length and residue-to-color mapping from all clues before filling; do not extrapolate from only the densest cluster.

Use when an ARC input has colored clues distributed on diagonals running down-right and the output appears to expand them into a periodic pattern.

4. Fill each cell `(r,c)` with the color mapped to `(c-r) mod period`; preserve the input dimensions.
5. Verify all nonzero clue cells match the generated grid.

## Pitfalls
- The relevant lines are down-right diagonals, where `c-r` is constant—not rows, columns, or down-left diagonals.
- Do not assume the cycle length equals the grid width. Look for the smallest period that matches all clue colors.
- Determine the mapping from every clue before filling; a partial stripe sequence may not expose the whole cycle.
